newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian shareholder problems remain post-Mosenergo.
newsitem.headline: Russian shareholder problems remain post-Mosenergo.

text.p: Danger still lurks across Russia for foreign shareholders even though reformist ministers rescued investors whose voting rights at utility Mosenergo were nearly limited this week.

Foreign shareholders still risk having their stakes diluted and face problems with voting and representation, among other issues, equity analysts said on Tuesday. But many analysts say the risks are shrinking.
Shareholder conflicts are the rule rather than the exception in Russia, said Joseph Blasi, a Rutgers University professor whose team is studying the country's 100 largest companies.
"Every company is involved in a shareholder conflict, whether under-the-surface tension, a lawsuit or a dispute of some kind," he said of the 100 companies.
Mosenergo's board of directors dropped proposals to limit shareholder voting rights from the agenda of this week's annual meeting, a move which analysts attributed to government intervention.

New reformers were seen twisting the arm of national utility Unified Energy System (UES), which owns 49 percent of Mosenergo and which successfully forced through limits to voting rights at another regional utility last year.

"The not-so-discrete intervention of First Deputy Premier Boris Nemtsov... bodes well for aggressive protection of shareholder rights under the new-look cabinet," Renaissance Capital investment bank wrote.
"This is a very encouraging demonstration of political will by the reorganised government," said Christopher Granville, who is United City Bank's director of research.
Nemtsov was appointed in a recent cabinet reshuffle which swept young reformers to power.
Mosenergo also postponed plans for a potentially dilutive share issue. But legislation and enforcement of shareholders' rights are so far limited, Russia's securities watchdog says.

"There is not a whole lot the commission can do if there was a violation of joint stock companies law," said Kristen Staples, director of communications at the Federal Commission for the Securities Market.
The commission has broad powers to withdraw brokers' licences but can only appeal to companies under joint stock company law, she said.
In December the commission resolved a dilutive share issue by Surgutneftegaz, an oil company.
Surgut Holding, which had bought the entire issue below market price, paid an additional sum, a move welcomed by some analysts although the price was still below the market level.

Staples said the victory was possible only with help from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, which was considering an application by Surgut for American Depositary Receipts to trade in the United States.
"For other companies over which we do not have that leverage there is not so much we can do," she said.

Shareholders holding 40 percent of Novolipetsk Metallurgical Plant, one of Russia's largest steel makers, have tried for over a year to gain representation on the board of directors and are currently in court.
"The commission can make a recommendation to the court, but according to the criminal code the company is not punishable," said Staples.

Blasi said Novolipetsk was not unusual but Peter Halloran, who is head of equities and research at CS First Boston, said the steel combine problem was an anomaly. Shareholder rights were improving as companies opened up and the government considered new legislation, he said.

CSFB owns stakes in a number of companies across Russia but Halloran said it had not had to enforce its rights legally. "On paper it would look extremely problematic, but in reality we have found very few problems voting our shares," he said.
Companies themselves responded to investors. "Increasingly
companies are looking to the West and understanding what a capital market is and what it brings," he said.
Staples said the commission was petitioning for the right to levy fines and extend its enforcement powers.
Halloran expected the new reformers who came to the aid of Mosenergo shareholders to strengthen legislation as well as using their influence behind the scenes.
"I think they will introduce a series of new laws. They have in mind to improve the privatisation schedule and you can't do that without a healthy capital market environment," he said.
